title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) to test whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration versus plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes (model_calls_used = 301) and produced baseline = 299/300 valid configurations (99.667%) and guarded = 300/300 valid configurations (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole initially invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered power calculation assumed a planning baseline pass rate = 0.40 and targeted a 50% relative reduction in fail rate; the observed near‑ceiling baseline invalidates that planning assumption. We report preregistered design, execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, post‑hoc inferential sensitivity grounded in archived contingency counts, and artifact‑grounded operational and methodological recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. Execution and analysis artifacts are archived with the run.

sections.introduction:
Automating high‑level operator intent into device configuration accelerates NetOps but raises operational risk when generated changes are misordered, incomplete, or unsafe. Current literature and architectural proposals converge on generate→verify→repair patterns combining probabilistic generators (LLMs) with deterministic validators to reduce misconfiguration risk. However, rigorous preregistered A/B experiments that quantify first‑pass misconfiguration reductions for bounded guarded pipelines remain scarce.

This study implements a narrowly scoped preregistered paired experiment that evaluates a minimal guarded pipeline: one shared LLM candidate per task (single‑shot generation), a frozen deterministic validator that performs rule‑ and dependency‑based checks, and at most one automated repair attempt when the validator detects violations. Our core research question is: Can this minimal guarded pipeline reduce first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation under a controlled paired design? Contributions are: (1) a preregistered confirmatory paired experiment (N=300) with deterministic seed generation and full archival of model outputs, validator traces, and repair traces; (2) an evidence‑grounded analysis showing that the observed near‑ceiling baseline undermined preregistered power assumptions; and (3) operational and methodological recommendations (task difficulty calibration, paired sampling semantics, repair budget design) for future confirmatory NetOps evaluations.
sections.related_work: Surveys and system papers show that LLMs can synthesize network configuration templates from intent but exhibit failure modes—hallucination, misordering, and overconfidence—that threaten operational safety. Empirical and conceptual work outside NetOps shows that retrieval augmentation, deterministic verifiers, and repair loops reduce factual errors and improve grounding; architectural proposals for NetOps recommend deterministic validators as floor‑safety nets and generate→verify→repair pipelines for agentic workflows (see representative works cited). Despite these convergent recommendations, we found few preregistered paired A/B experiments that (a) use a deterministically generated task bank, (b) fix a frozen validator implementation, and (c) bound the automated repair budget for inference about first‑pass misconfiguration rate. Our study addresses that controlled gap and positions its contributions relative to the closest operationally motivated proposals and empirical demonstrations.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypotheses: The study was preregistered (study_id: cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) before execution. The preregistration record (checksum recorded in the execution manifest) specified confirmatory H1: the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus plain single‑shot generation, and H2: one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40 for planning the detectable effect size and sample size.

Design and sampling semantics: We used a paired within‑task design with 300 deterministically generated seeds from the frozen task generator. For each seed the same sampled LLM candidate (generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate") was shared between both arms: baseline (single‑shot generation) and guarded (the same candidate validated and, if invalid, subjected to up to one automated repair attempt). The preregistered choice to reuse the same candidate per pair increases within‑pair correlation and therefore reduces the number of informative discordant pairs available to McNemar inference; this pairing semantics was recorded in the preregistration and is material to power and interpretation.

Model, validator, and runtime constraints: The declared model in the execution contract was gpt-5-mini. The frozen deterministic validator/repair adapter (validator id deterministic_netops_validator_v5) performed syntactic canonicalization, AST parsing, rule‑ and dependency‑based constraint checks, and produced normalized configurations and violation codes used for binary pass/fail scoring. The preregistered execution contract fixed initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1 and maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; a global model‑call budget and retry policy were specified. Planned episodes = 600 (two episodes per seed); actual execution used 301 model calls because shared initial generation was counted once per pair and only a single repair call occurred across the run.

Scoring and estimands: The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline computed from binary pass/fail outcomes assigned by the deterministic validator. The preregistered primary test was the exact McNemar two‑sided test (α=0.05) on paired outcomes. A paired bootstrap percentile CI for the absolute paired difference (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) was prespecified to accompany the point estimate. Secondary analyses included repair success with exact binomial intervals and sensitivity analyses for missingness and contamination; multiplicity for exploratory analyses was controlled as preregistered.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: Planned episodes = 600, completed episodes = 600, complete pairs = 300, model_calls_used = 301, repair calls invoked = 1. No provider or infrastructure failures occurred under the preregistered retry policy; contamination checks flagged no deterministic exact duplicates among preregistered seeds and no exclusions or replacements were executed. These execution summary facts are recorded in the archived execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle.

Primary outcomes and contingency counts (archive‑derived): baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency counts are n11 = 299 (both success), n10 = 1 (guarded success, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (guarded fail, baseline success), n00 = 0 (both fail). These counts are the source material for all confirmatory statistics and appear in the archived paired_contingency_table artifact.

Statistical inference: The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test on the observed contingency yields p = 1.00. The absolute paired difference estimate (guarded minus baseline success rate) = 0.0033333333 (1/300). The paired bootstrap (percentile) 95% CI for the absolute paired difference = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729), as reported in the archived analysis artifacts. Repair outcomes (H2): the single allowed automated repair call corrected the only initially invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1); the Clopper–Pearson exact 95% CI for this numerator/denominator is [0.025, 1.0].

Post‑hoc inferential sensitivity: The observed discordant pair total (n10 + n01 = 1) constrains the resolvable absolute paired difference: a single discordant pair among 300 pairs corresponds to the point estimate 1/300 ≈ 0.003333. With only one discordant pair the exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.00 under the standard small‑count calculation because the test cannot exclude symmetric chance for that single discordance under the null. Practically, the preregistered planning target (~+0.30 absolute) is orders of magnitude larger than the empirical resolvable improvement in this run; the observed near‑ceiling baseline therefore invalidates the preregistered power assumption and prevents confirmatory support for the preregistered effect size.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and operational implications: The guarded pipeline corrected the single observed invalid baseline output, demonstrating that the implemented deterministic validator plus a single automated repair iteration can remediate some validator‑detected violations. However, because the baseline pass rate was far higher than planned, the run provides no evidence that the guarded pipeline yields the large preregistered effect (≥50% relative reduction in fail rate). Two important operational lessons follow.

First, task difficulty calibration is essential. Confirmatory designs targeting substantial absolute improvements must ensure the baseline failure prevalence leaves statistical headroom. Our preregistered planning assumed baseline pass rate = 0.40; obtaining an empirical baseline near 1.0 eliminates detectability for large preregistered effects. Practically, experimenters should either design or adversarially augment task banks to produce meaningful baseline failure prevalence or choose estimands conditional on initial failure (e.g., repair effectiveness) rather than absolute population‑level risk reduction.

Second, pairing semantics and repair budgets shape inference. Reusing a shared initial candidate per pair reduces potential discordant pairs for McNemar inference; independent generation across arms increases discordant‑pair potential but introduces cross‑arm heterogeneity and may require larger N. Likewise, restricting automated repair to a single iteration bounds operational realism—production guardrails often permit multiple repair attempts plus human approval. Future confirmatory studies should preregister generation semantics and repair budgets aligned with the operational deployment model and plan sample sizes to secure a prespecified number of initial failures for precise estimation.

Threats to validity and generality: Internal validity is affected by the shared_initial_candidate pairing choice (increasing within‑pair correlation). Construct validity is limited because validator checks operate on canonicalized configurations rather than full dynamic emulation; we did not execute packet‑level or runtime reachability tests. External validity is constrained by the synthetic task bank, constrained vendor‑template scope, a single model family (gpt-5-mini), and a single validator implementation. Conclusion validity is limited by the small number of informative discordant pairs; statistical inference about large preregistered effects is therefore unsupported by the observed data.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired experiment (N=300 pairs) using a frozen deterministic validator and a one‑iteration automated repair budget applied to gpt‑5‑mini outputs, baseline single‑shot generation was near‑ceiling (299/300) and the guarded pipeline produced 300/300 valid outputs. The single automated repair corrected the only observed invalid baseline output, but the run does not support the preregistered claim of ≥50% relative reduction in misconfiguration because the observed baseline contradicted the planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40) and left no statistical headroom. We recommend that future confirmatory NetOps evaluations (1) calibrate task difficulty to produce a predetermined number of initial failures, (2) preregister generation semantics (shared vs independent draws) and repair budgets aligned to deployment expectations, and (3) measure runtime semantic effects (emulation or simulation) when operational claims require runtime guarantees. All archived artifacts referenced in this paper accompany the run to support reproducibility and method refinement.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.
The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicts that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.

Sampling semantics (generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate") reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
